title: Reversing and merging lists
sub: Reverse Linked List and Merge Two Sorted Lists: three pointers, recursion and its stack, the dummy node
cards/0/title: The list node and the reversal problem
cards/0/body:
In LeetCode problems in C#, a list is made of ListNode class nodes with val and next fields; the last node points to null. A class, not a struct: a node refers to a node of its own type.

Reverse Linked List (LeetCode #206, core). Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 becomes 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. From 0 to 5000 nodes. The follow-up in the statement: do it both iteratively and recursively.

What is being tested here is not an algorithm but pointer hygiene. Almost every list problem at an interview is like this: rewire the links in the right order, do not lose the tail, do not forget the empty list and the single node. Signals: “in place”, “O(1) memory”, “rearrange the nodes, not the values”.
cards/1/title: Naive solutions: a stack of nodes and an array of values
cards/1/body:
A stack of nodes. Push all nodes onto a Stack<ListNode> and pop them, linking in order: the first one popped is the new head. O(n) time and O(n) memory. The trap at the end: the former head is now the tail, but its next still points to the second node — without tail.next = null you get a cycle.

An array of values. Copy the vals into an array and write them back in reverse. Also O(n) memory, and worse: it changes the values, not the nodes. If something outside refers to the nodes (an “id → node” dictionary, as in an LRU cache), or a node holds an object with data rather than a single number, such a “reversal” silently scrambles the data.

Both solutions are honest and worth naming as a baseline. But the interviewer will almost always ask for O(1) extra memory.
cards/2/q: Why is “copy the values into an array and write them back into the nodes in reverse” usually not accepted?
cards/2/options/0: It takes O(n) memory, and it changes values rather than nodes: outside references to the nodes will point at someone else’s data
cards/2/options/1: It is O(n²): writing a value into the k-th node means walking from the head every time
cards/2/explain: The task is to rearrange the nodes with O(1) memory. The array is an extra O(n), and writing values instead of rewiring links breaks anything that holds a reference to a node: a node dictionary, data inside the node, another list sharing the tail.
cards/2/wrong/1: You can write in a single pass from the head while reading the array from the end — that is O(n). The problem is memory and swapped values, not time.
cards/2/wrong/2: The values are just copied; the sign does not matter.
cards/3/title: The idea: three pointers, one arrow per step
cards/3/body:
Walk the list once and reverse one arrow per step. You need three pointers: prev — the head of the part already reversed, cur — the first node not yet touched, next — a spare reference to the tail.

A step is four assignments, and their order matters: 1) next = cur.next — save the tail while the link to it is intact; 2) cur.next = prev — reverse the arrow; 3) prev = cur; 4) cur = next. Swap 1 and 2 and the only link to the tail is overwritten before it was saved.

Invariant: before each step prev is the reversed prefix, cur is the untouched suffix, and there are no arrows between them. The loop ends at cur == null, and the new head is prev. The empty list and a single node need no special cases. Time O(n), memory O(1).
cards/4/explain: The loop runs while there is an untouched node: with cur.next != null the last node is never reversed. First save the tail with next = cur.next, then point the arrow at prev, then move on to the saved next. The new head is prev: by the end head points to the former first node, which is now the tail.
cards/5/task: Step through 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. The rig stops twice: in the middle of the reversal and at the very end.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: prev = 2, cur = 3. Where does the code point the arrow 3.next?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: First next = 4 is saved, then 3.next = prev = 2. The reversed part grows: 3 → 2 → 1 → null; nodes 4 → 5 are still untouched, and the only link to 4 is in next.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: The last step reversed the arrow 5 → 4, and now cur = null. What does the code return?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: cur == null marks the end, and the head of the reversed list is prev, node 5. head still points to 1, which is now the tail with 1.next = null: returning head means returning a one-node list.
cards/6/q: On 1 → 2 → 3 this code returns a list with the single node 1. Tap the line after which the tail of the list is lost.
cards/6/explain: cur.next = prev overwrites the only link to node 2 before it was saved. On the first step 1.next = null, then next = cur.next = null, the loop ends, and 1 is returned without its tail. The order is: first var next = cur.next, then cur.next = prev.
cards/7/title: The recursive version and its stack
cards/7/body:
The follow-up is “and recursively?”. The recursion first reverses the tail and then attaches the current node to the end of the reversed part. head.next is the former second node, now the last one in the reversed tail, so head.next.next = head. And head.next = null is mandatory: otherwise the first and second nodes point at each other.

The cost: O(n) time, but also O(n) memory — one call-stack frame per node. On 5000 nodes that is fine; on a list of 10⁶ nodes it is a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught in .NET. C# does not promise to turn tail recursion into a loop, and this recursion is not even a tail call: there is work left after the call.

At an interview, write both and say why production code uses the iterative one: the same time complexity, O(1) memory and no limit on length.
cards/8/q: The line head.next = null was removed from the recursive version. What happens on 1 → 2 → 3?
cards/8/options/0: The head is 3, but nodes 1 and 2 point at each other: walking the list never ends
cards/8/options/1: The correct list 3 → 2 → 1: the line was redundant
cards/8/explain: The call for 2 sets 3.next = 2, while 2.next stays 3. The call for 1 sets 2.next = 1, while 1.next stays 2. Result: 3 → 2 → 1 → 2 → 1 … — a cycle. head.next = null at each level cuts the old forward arrow.
cards/8/wrong/1: The old forward arrow does not go anywhere: without clearing it the former head has 1.next = 2, while 2.next is already 1.
cards/8/wrong/2: head.next.next runs only when head.next != null — the base case guarantees it. There is no crash, there is a cycle.
cards/9/title: Merge Two Sorted Lists: the dummy node
cards/9/body:
Merge Two Sorted Lists (LeetCode #21). Two sorted lists of 0–50 nodes each; merge them into one sorted list made of their own nodes. This is the merge step of merge sort: compare the heads, attach the smaller one to the result, move on.

The dummy node. The awkward part is the head of the result: while nothing is attached there is nothing to attach to, so the first iteration would have to be written separately. Create a dummy before the future head and a tail pointer to the last attached node. Then every step is the same: tail.next = smaller; tail = tail.next, and the answer is dummy.next. The same trick removes the special case “delete the head itself” in the next lesson.

The remainder. Once one list runs out, attach the other whole, with a single link — tail.next = a ?? b, no loop: it is already sorted. On equal values take from a (<=) — the merge is stable, equal elements keep their order. An empty input list is not a special case either: the loop runs zero times and the other list is attached whole. Time O(n + m), memory O(1): no new nodes except one dummy.
cards/9/deep:
Without a dummy: a reference to a reference. C# has no pointer to a pointer, but it has ref locals, and since C# 7.3 they can be reassigned. ref ListNode link = ref head; is “the slot where the next node goes”: first the head variable itself, then the next field of the last node. A step is link = smaller; link = ref link.next;. No dummy node and no special case for the head; it compiles in C# 9, so in Unity too.

Recursive merge is shorter — if (a.val <= b.val) { a.next = Merge(a.next, b); return a; } — but costs O(n + m) stack. On 50 + 50 nodes it does not matter; on long lists it carries the same overflow risk as the recursive reversal.

Sorting a list (Sort List, #148) is merge sort: find the middle with fast and slow pointers (next lesson), sort the halves, merge them with this function. O(n log n) time and no copying into an array. LinkedList<T> in .NET has no sort — the usual way is to copy into an array, sort it and rebuild.

k lists (Merge k Sorted Lists, #23) use a heap of heads, O(N log k); that is the heaps unit.
cards/10/q: Assemble the merge of two sorted lists with a dummy node.
cards/10/explain: A node was taken from a — advance a. tail moves to the node just attached. After the loop at least one list is empty, and the rest of the other is already sorted: a ?? b attaches it with a single link (null would lose the tail). dummy is a helper node with value 0; the head of the result is dummy.next.
cards/11/q: Merging two sorted lists with a dummy. Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: With the condition a.val <= b.val, equal values from a come before those from b
cards/11/options/1: Once a runs out, the rest of b is attached with a single link, no loop
cards/11/options/2: The solution needs O(n + m) extra memory for new nodes
cards/11/options/3: Without a dummy you would have to pick the head of the result separately before the loop
cards/11/options/4: If one of the lists is empty, you need a separate if before the loop
cards/11/explain: On equality we take from a — equal elements keep their order. The remainder is already sorted and is attached whole. Nodes are reused, the only new one is dummy: O(1) memory. The dummy is exactly what removes the head special case. An empty list is not special either: the loop runs zero times, and tail.next = a ?? b returns the other list.
cards/12/q: You are reversing a list out loud at an interview. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: the list is singly linked, may be empty, rearrange the nodes, not the values
cards/12/items/1: Name the naive approach: a stack of nodes or an array of values — O(n) memory
cards/12/items/2: Idea: one pass, reverse one arrow per step; prev is reversed, cur is untouched
cards/12/items/3: Write the code: save next, reverse the arrow, move prev and cur
cards/12/items/4: Run 1 → 2 → 3 on paper, arrow by arrow
cards/12/items/5: State the complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory; recursion costs O(n) stack
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: the empty list and a single node go through without special branches
cards/12/explain: First the problem and the baseline, then the idea with its invariant, the code with the right order of assignments, a run, the complexity of both versions, and edge cases.
cards/13/q: Match the problem with the technique.
cards/13/pairs/0/0: Reverse a list in O(1) memory
cards/13/pairs/0/1: prev, cur, next: save, reverse, advance
cards/13/pairs/2/1: dummy and tail, the remainder with a single link
cards/13/pairs/3/0: Avoid a separate case for the head
cards/13/pairs/3/1: A dummy node before the head
